tagline.text: A museum of shoe stories from the Philippines' shoe capital

location.label: Location
location.text: J.P. Rizal Street, San Roque, Marikina City

children.text: This shoe museum occupies an old stone building near Marikina City Hall. It shows Imelda Marcos's shoes, shoes of past presidents and celebrities, a history of footwear around the world, and shoemaking tools, all in one place.

The Marikina Shoe Museum (Museo ng Sapatos in Filipino) is a small museum on J.P. Rizal Street in Marikina City, on the eastern side of Metro Manila. Marikina is nicknamed the "Shoe Capital of the Philippines," and the museum opened on February 16, 2001 to present the city's shoemaking industry and shoe culture. It was first called the Marikina Footwear Museum, and Wikipedia and a travel blog report that Imelda Marcos herself led the opening ceremony.

The most eye-catching exhibit here is the shoe collection of former First Lady Imelda Marcos. According to Wikipedia, the collection was seized by the Presidential Commission on Good Government (PCGG), displayed for about six years at the Malacañang Palace Museum under the Corazon Aquino government, then put into storage early in the Ramos administration. In 1996 the city of Marikina (under Mayor Bayani Fernando) asked for part of it, and it became the core of the museum. About 749 pairs were reportedly on display as of 2020. That number varies by source (local guides mention "more than 250 pairs"), and how the collection is presented is controversial, so we suggest reading the exhibit texts alongside the historical background and viewing it critically.

Beyond the shoes, the building itself is worth a look. It is a stone building from the late Spanish colonial period; Wikipedia gives the 1860s, while a travel blog says it was built in the 1880s as a rice warehouse by Doña Teresa de la Paz of the Tuason family, so the dates differ. It is said to have served afterward as a Spanish arsenal, a detention center during the Philippine–American War, a motor pool under American rule and a place of detention during the Japanese occupation, and after World War II as the Tuason family's rice mill. Several layers of modern Philippine history are stacked in a single building.

The Marikina River Park, a church and the shoe-factory street are all close by, so the museum combines well with a half-day city walk. The museum itself takes only an hour or two to see, so it fits into a half-day away from your Manila itinerary. About

from the museum entrance is the Marikina Cultural Center (Sentrong Pangkultura ng Marikina), so it is easy to see both together. It is a municipal museum and not large, but it is enough to understand at a glance why this city became famous for shoes.

Imelda Marcos's shoes are shown in glass cases along the mezzanine wall. About 749 pairs (size 8.5) were reported as of 2020, including pieces by designers such as Charles Jourdan, Christian Dior, Gucci and Oleg Cassini, along with a Filipiniana dress and Ferdinand Marcos's barong tagalog. Keep in mind that there is controversy over the meaning of the collection.

You will find shoes of former presidents Ferdinand Marcos, Manuel Roxas, Gloria Macapagal Arroyo and Fidel Ramos, as well as shoes donated by Joseph Estrada (size 10). Bowling shoes of Paeng Nepomuceno, shoes of beauty queens and entertainers, and the shoes Miriam Defensor Santiago wore in her 1992 campaign are also reported to be on display.

blocks.title: A history of shoes around the world

children.text: Replicas and displays show footwear through the ages, from the shoes of the Iceman around 3300 BC to Dutch clogs, Viking boots, Roman sandals and Indian moccasins. It is an easy-to-follow exhibit for families with children as well.
There are cobbler's tools, a Singer sewing machine, shoe lasts, shoe components, men's and ladies' shoe stands, a manual delaster and a leather shoe about
1 m
high. The tools and processes explain how Marikina became a shoe city.
Winning entries from the city's annual shoe design competition are on display. Most are imaginative fantasy shoes that look nothing like everyday footwear.

On the sidewalk in front of the museum is Shoe-perstar Alley, which opened on November 13, 2012 during the Sapatos Festival. Forty-nine brass shoe tiles set into the pavement honor people who contributed to Marikina's shoe industry, so you can walk along and look for the names.

In front of the museum stood an acacia tree about a hundred years old, which was uprooted by a tornado during Typhoon Ompong in September 2018. Revived with first aid and bonsai techniques, it is now a tree that symbolizes the resilience of the community.

The building began as a rice warehouse and arsenal in the Spanish colonial period and later served as a detention center, a motor pool and a rice mill, so its walls and roof structure are sights in themselves. There is also a record that during Typhoon Ondoy in 2009 the interior was flooded to about
(4 feet), and many shoes were damaged.
Get off at LRT-2 Santolan station, take a jeepney bound for San Mateo and get off at City Hall on Central Shoe Avenue. The museum is a short walk away.
Enter the museum. Go through the Imelda Marcos display, the shoes of presidents and celebrities, the history of shoes around the world and the shoemaking tools in order.
See Shoe-perstar Alley and the acacia tree in front of the museum, then look around the Marikina Cultural Center, about
away.
Walk along J.P. Rizal Street to see the church (Our Lady of the Abandoned Parish).
Have lunch at a restaurant in downtown Marikina.
Walk through Marikina River Park or rent a bicycle and stroll along the river.
The museum is air-conditioned, but Marikina is hot and humid in the daytime, so you can also leave the riverside walk until after the afternoon heat, around sunset.

items.title: Church and riverside route
items.subtitle: From the shoe street to the riverside park

children.text: After the museum, walk along J.P. Rizal Street to the Diocesan Shrine and Parish of Our Lady of the Abandoned. The Baroque-style church has religious murals and an organ that is best heard on Sundays.
Pass by Gibson's Shoe Factory and think about Marikina's shoemaking tradition. It is said to be open Monday–Saturday
, but check first whether you can look inside.
Have lunch and rest at a restaurant downtown.
Move on to Marikina River Park and walk along the river or rent a bicycle. It also has a Roman-style garden and a Filipino-Chinese friendship pagoda.
Buy snacks at the stalls around sunset and head back.
The church is a place of worship, so visit quietly and dress modestly. Its hours are listed as 4:00 AM to 9:00 PM, but please check.

items.title: From Manila by LRT and jeepney

children.text: Get off at Santolan station, the terminus of LRT-2. Riding LRT-2 from central Manila is the simplest way.
From outside Santolan station, take a San Mateo-bound jeepney, get off at City Hall on Central Shoe Avenue and walk to the museum.
Travel time and fares vary with the time of day and traffic, so check locally.
You can go by Grab or taxi from central Manila, Makati and Quezon City. The Marikina stretch can be congested during rush hours.
Set the destination as "Marikina Shoe Museum, J.P. Rizal St."
Short distances in downtown Marikina can be covered on foot, and tricycles are also available.
From the museum to Marikina River Park, a tricycle is convenient if your group is large.

The museum is indoors, but if you want to combine it with a city walk and the riverside park, the dry season from November to May is best. December to February is especially pleasant, as it is relatively cool for walking.

During the rainy season from June to November, typhoons and heavy rain can flood the area around the Marikina River. The museum was flooded during Typhoon Ondoy in 2009, so postpone your plans when a typhoon warning is in effect.

and may vary with local conditions.
There are not many large restaurants around the museum, so many visitors eat downtown or at SM City Marikina (on Marikina-Infanta Highway). The mall is listed as open Sunday–Thursday
and Friday–Saturday
, with cafés, stores and a cinema, so it is a good place to cool off. Marikina River Park is reported to have food stalls in the evening where you can buy snacks.

There is lodging in Marikina too, but most travelers stay in central Manila, Quezon City or Pasig and visit as a day trip. A realistic plan is to move on to Quezon City or BGC for dinner after visiting the museum.

Hours differ by source (opening between 7:30 and 8:00 AM, closing between 4:30 and 5:00 PM), so check with the Marikina City tourism office (tel. (632) 696-6516) or the city hall announcements before you go.
The Imelda Marcos collection is politically controversial, so read the exhibit explanations critically and compare them with local historical material.
The Marikina Cultural Center is about
from the museum, so see both on the same day.
Taking a jeepney from Santolan station is the cheapest way. Tell the jeepney driver that you are getting off at "City Hall."
If you are interested in buying shoes, stop by local shoe shops and shoe factories such as Gibson's. Prices and quality differ from shop to shop.
The museum is indoors and shelters you from the sun, but there is some walking, so wear comfortable shoes.
Check photography rules locally.
The church stands at the corner of J.P. Rizal Street and V. Gomez Street, so it is easy to walk there from the museum.
Marikina River Park is listed as open 24 hours, but do not go alone at night; use it while it is light.
Marikina often floods during typhoons and heavy rain. The inside of the museum was also badly flooded during Typhoon Ondoy in 2009, so check the weather forecast in the rainy season.
Opening hours and admission differ between sources, so check locally. Also check directly whether a separate foreigner rate exists.
The Imelda Marcos collection is a politically sensitive subject. Opinions may differ when you talk with local people.
During rush hours, the roads to Marikina and the area around Santolan station are very congested.
When riding jeepneys and tricycles, keep your belongings in front of you.
Check the announcements on the Marikina City official channels for the latest operating status.
The whole city where the museum stands is famous for its shoe industry and culture. A city walk and the riverside park combine well with it.
A park running about
11 km
along the river, with jogging, cycling and walking routes and stalls that open in the evening. Bicycles can reportedly be rented for about

blocks.title: Our Lady of the Abandoned Parish

children.text: A Baroque-style church at the corner of J.P. Rizal Street and V. Gomez Street. You can see it next along the same street as the museum.
A military and safety shoe factory on J.P. Rizal Street, operating since 1945, said to be open Monday–Saturday from 8:00 to 17:00. Check first whether visits are possible.
